explanations.answer: Moses already gave them land east of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "For Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes." Their slice was already off the tray before the lot-drawing started. Nobody was left out of the line, they had just been served early.

explanations.answer: They will get the land left over at the end
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, friend. Nothing in the text says anything about leftovers. It says Moses had already given them their inheritance east of the Jordan (Joshua 14:3). Their land was settled, so the lot only had to cover the other nine and a half tribes.

explanations.answer: They have to win their land in battle first
explanations.explanation: Close, but this passage mentions no battle for them. Joshua 14:3 says Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes. So the lot only had to cover the nine and a half. The text gives Moses' gift as the reason, friend, and nothing about a fight.

Cities it is. The text says no portion of the land went to the Levites, "…except for cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." So the Levites had places to live and room for their animals. Not a bad deal, baker.

Tents is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. Joshua 14:4 says the Levites got "…cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." So the text gives them cities, plus pasturelands for their animals. No tent shows up on that list.

Caves, huh? Joshua 14:4 says the Levites got "…cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." So their homes were cities, and their animals had pasture. No caves on that list, baker. I know a thing or two about dark, dusty spots, and this isn't one of them.

explanations.answer: He remained loyal to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Caleb says, "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." Right before that, he says his brothers who went with him made the hearts of the people melt with fear. Joshua 14:8 sets those two things side by side, and Caleb puts himself on the loyal side. That's a line worth hanging onto.

explanations.answer: He stayed quiet in the camp
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Caleb never says he stayed quiet. He says Moses sent him to spy out the land and he brought "…an honest report." (Joshua 14:7). Then he says, "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:8). I think quiet would have been the easy road, but that's not the road he describes.

explanations.answer: He went back to spy again
explanations.explanation: A second spy trip would mean a lot more walking, baker, but Caleb doesn't mention one. He says Moses sent him to spy out the land and he brought back "…an honest report." (Joshua 14:7). Then he says, "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:8). Loyalty is what he claims, not a return visit.

explanations.answer: The land his feet had walked on
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:9). Notice the reason Moses gives, baker. Caleb had wholly followed the LORD, and the promise was attached to the ground under his feet.

The Jordan is a reasonable guess, friend, but the verse doesn't point to a river at all. Moses swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever…" (Joshua 14:9). The land is named by where Caleb had set foot. That's the detail to hold onto.

Gilgal is where the sons of Judah approach Joshua (Joshua 14:6), so I see the pull, baker. But Moses' oath doesn't name Gilgal. He swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever…" (Joshua 14:9). The promise points to where Caleb had set foot.
Eighty-five, and Caleb says so himself: "…here I am today, eighty-five years old…" Forty plus forty-five does it. Math works even when the oven's on, baker.

So close, friend. Forty plus forty-five lands on eighty-five, and Caleb says it himself: "…here I am today, eighty-five years old…" (Joshua 14:10). You were five years short. I once lost count of how long I sat in a drawer, so no judgment here.

Ninety overshoots by five, baker. Forty plus forty-five is eighty-five, and Caleb says it himself: "…here I am today, eighty-five years old…" (Joshua 14:10). Honestly, I'd have probably said ninety too. I count cookies by tapping the box and losing my place, so my math has been running hot for years.

True. Caleb says he's "…still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out." Then he adds, "As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in." Eighty-five and ready to go, baker. I'm over here stretching just to reach the top shelf.

It's actually true, friend. Caleb says he's "…still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out." He goes on, "As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in." (Joshua 14:11). He doesn't say he's slowed down at all.

Right, baker. Caleb says, "Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." Just before, he tells Joshua he's still strong for war (Joshua 14:11). He also names the Anakim's great and fortified cities. And when he talks about driving them out, he names the LORD's help.

Joshua is standing right there, so I see why you'd think so. But Caleb never mentions an army. He says, "Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." (Joshua 14:12). The help he names is the LORD's.

A siege would be a very patient plan, friend. But Caleb doesn't mention one. He says, "Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." (Joshua 14:12). The only help he names is the LORD's.
Not true, baker. Joshua doesn't turn Caleb down. The text says, "Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance." Caleb asked and Caleb got a blessing with it.
False is right. Joshua doesn't send Caleb away. "Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance." He got the blessing and the land, friend.

Anakim is right. The text says Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, "…after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." Those are the same Anakim Caleb mentioned earlier, with their great and fortified cities (Joshua 14:12). Fancy name, baker, but Hebron suits it better.

Amorites is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the name in this verse. It says Kiriath-arba was named "…after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." (Joshua 14:15). The Anakim are the people Caleb mentions back in verse 12, with their great and fortified cities.

Philistines is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name in this verse. It says Kiriath-arba was named "…after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." (Joshua 14:15). Caleb mentions the Anakim in verse 12, along with their great and fortified cities.
